Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Regret Optimization for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

Yikai Wang    Shang Liu    Jose Blanchet
1Department of Statistics and Operations Research, University of North Carolina
2Imperial Business School, Imperial College London
3Department of Management Science and Engineering, Stanford University
Abstract

Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is a central post-training tool for aligning large language models, but its training reward is only a learned proxy for true human utility. This creates a decision problem under objective misspecification: the policy is optimized against an estimated reward, while deployment performance is governed by an unobserved population preference. The resulting gap leads to reward over-optimization, where proxy reward keeps improving after true quality deteriorates. We propose distributionally robust regret optimization (DRRO) for RLHF with a Wasserstein ambiguity set over reward laws, using promptwise ℓp\ell_{p} distances between reward vectors as transport costs. Unlike standard distributionally robust optimization, which pessimizes worst-case value, DRRO pessimizes worst-case regret relative to the best policy under the same plausible reward perturbation. We show that the expressive-policy problem decomposes into promptwise regret problems. For each prompt, the inner adversary has a dual-norm closed form; under the ℓ1\ell_{1} transport cost used by our algorithm, the optimizer has a water-filling structure. These results lead to a practical policy-gradient algorithm that adds a simple sampled bonus to GRPO-style training. Theory and experiments both show that DRRO is less over-pessimistic than standard DRO and mitigates over-optimization more effectively than existing baselines.

**footnotetext: Equal contribution. Corresponding to s.liu21@imperial.ac.uk.

1 Introduction

Large language models owe much of their practical usefulness not only to scale, but also to post-training. Pretraining creates a strong next-token predictor, but not necessarily a model that is helpful, safe, or responsive to human intent. Modern alignment pipelines therefore add supervised fine-tuning and preference-based policy optimization, most prominently reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) (Christiano et al., 2017; Ziegler et al., 2019; Stiennon et al., 2020; Ouyang et al., 2022). In a typical RLHF pipeline, prompts are sampled, the model generates candidate responses, humans express preferences, a reward model is fit to those preferences, and the language model is optimized against the learned reward. The leverage of this stage is substantial: Ouyang et al. (2022) reported that a 1.3B aligned model was preferred by human raters to a 175B model without comparable RLHF.

The same pipeline also creates the problem studied in this paper. Direct human feedback is too expensive to collect in real time while policy optimization repeatedly samples massive numbers of responses. RLHF therefore trains a reward model to mimic human ratings. The Bradley–Terry comparison model is perhaps the most widely adopted approach (Bradley and Terry, 1952; Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022): for two responses to the same prompt, the preference probability is modeled through the difference between their learned rewards. This construction makes the central issue transparent. The learned reward score is not human preference itself; it is a proxy, estimated from finite and distribution-limited comparisons, and then optimized as if it were the objective. Goodhart’s law warns that when a measurement becomes a goal to optimize, the measurement may no longer be a good measurement (Goodhart, 1975; Strathern, 1997). RLHF places that warning directly inside a learning algorithm.

The empirical signature is now clear. In the controlled study of Gao et al. (2023), the proxy reward continued to improve as the policy moved farther from the initial model, while a stronger gold-standard reward first peaked and then deteriorated. The very signal used for training can therefore certify progress while actual quality is declining. Related evidence appears in studies of human-feedback confounders (Hosking et al., 2024), direct alignment over-optimization (Rafailov et al., 2024), and Goodhart effects in reinforcement learning (Karwowski et al., 2024).

Conceptually, fix a prompt and imagine listing all complete responses. Promptwise RLHF shifts probability mass toward responses with high learned proxy reward. Deployment quality, however, is governed by population preferences: different users may assign different latent rewards to the same response, and the relevant target is their aggregate preference rather than the learned score. Downstream RLHF is therefore decision making under objective misspecification. More importantly, the misspecification is decision-dependent: optimization changes the response distribution, which changes where the reward model is asked to extrapolate.

Existing mitigations broadly take two paths. One constrains the updated policy near an initial, reference, or behavior policy, through divergence-based or reference-policy control (Schulman et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022; Xiong et al., 2024), explicit constrained RLHF (Moskovitz et al., 2024), or behavior- and demonstration-supported regularization (Dai et al., 2025; Rita et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024). These safeguards can be useful, but they also suppress potentially valuable improvement and hide the deeper question of what objective should be optimized.

The other path improves the proxy itself, for example through reward-model ensembles (Coste et al., 2024; Eisenstein et al., 2024), iterative or active preference collection (Xiong et al., 2024; Das et al., 2024), alternative reward-model objectives (Miao et al., 2024), or robust reward modeling (Liu et al., 2025; Bukharin et al., 2025). These approaches address the right object, but typically require additional data, models, and/or training stages.

A natural alternative is to treat the reward model as an uncertain objective and import robust optimization. Standard distributionally robust optimization (DRO) evaluates a policy by its worst plausible reward model inside an ambiguity set around the learned reward model, drawing on a powerful operations research toolkit for robust and Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization (Ben-Tal et al., 2013; Wiesemann et al., 2014; Mohajerin Esfahani and Kuhn, 2018). In our setting, the Wasserstein distance is taken over reward laws, and the transport cost is the promptwise ℓp\ell_{p} distance between reward vectors.

Yet worst-case value is not always the right benchmark. Pessimistic value penalties and restrictive feasible regions can become over-conservative (Xu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Wolf et al., 2025); in our benchmark, standard DRO even performs worse than raw PPO in peak held-out gold reward, as detailed in the experiments. Inspired by regret in reinforcement learning (Jaksch et al., 2010; Jin et al., 2018), we argue that RLHF should not robustify absolute value alone. Here, regret means the gap between the chosen policy and the best policy that would have been chosen under the same realized plausible reward.

This motivates our central idea: robustify regret, not value. Distributionally robust regret optimization (DRRO) evaluates a policy by its worst plausible regret against the hindsight-best policy under the same plausible reward model. This benchmark is especially natural in RLHF because one policy must be committed before the realized user preference is observed.

The obstacle is computational. Worst-case regret is generally much harder to optimize than worst-case value: classical minmax-regret problems are NP-hard even in static settings (Averbakh, 2004; Averbakh and Lebedev, 2005), and recent ex-ante DRRO formulations often require substantial optimization machinery (Agarwal and Zhang, 2022; Cho and Yang, 2024; Bitar, 2024; Fiechtner and Blanchet, 2025). This seems discouraging for RLHF, where the action space is the set of all possible language-model responses.

The main theoretical message of this paper is that promptwise RLHF has far more structure than this pessimistic view suggests. For an expressive policy class, the global ex-ante problem decomposes into promptwise regret problems. Each fixed-prompt problem becomes a portfolio-style allocation over responses. Under Wasserstein ambiguity with promptwise ℓp\ell_{p} transport cost, the inner adversary has an explicit dual-norm form; under the ℓ1\ell_{1} transport cost used by our algorithm, the minimizer further collapses to a water-filling rule. This also explains why DRRO is less pessimistic than DRO: DRRO uses the proxy’s ranking information when deciding how to hedge, whereas DRO under the same formulation can ignore it. As ambiguity shrinks, DRRO recovers proxy-greedy behavior; as ambiguity grows, it converges to the uniform policy.

Closed-form promptwise solutions are insightful, but not yet an RLHF algorithm. The full response simplex is hidden and astronomically large, and the trainable object is the LLM parameter vector rather than an explicit probability table. We therefore derive policy-gradient surrogates for DRRO, show that the robust correction appears as a simple reward bonus, and replace the exact maximum by a smooth maximum estimated from sampled responses through self-normalized importance sampling. With numerically stable group-normalized rollout probabilities, the resulting method requires only minimal changes to GRPO implementations (Shao et al., 2024) and gives the strongest over-optimization mitigation among the baselines we test.

Contributions.

The paper makes five contributions.

  1. (a)

    Formulation. We formulate RLHF under reward-model misspecification as an ex-ante DRRO problem with Wasserstein ambiguity over reward laws and promptwise ℓp\ell_{p} transport costs.

  2. (b)

    Promptwise theory. We prove promptwise decomposition, derive dual-norm closed-form adversaries, and obtain a water-filling optimal policy under the ℓ1\ell_{1} transport cost used by the algorithm.

  3. (c)

    Algorithm. We turn the exact theory into policy-gradient surrogates, a sampling-based smooth-maximum estimator, a stable group-normalized implementation, and ambiguity-budget rules.

  4. (d)

    Experiments. On a matched VERL benchmark, soft dynamic DRRO reaches peak held-out gold reward 1.43, compared with 1.27 for GRPO, 1.20 for PPO, and 0.79 for DRO.

  5. (e)

    DRO comparison. We show theoretically that DRRO can be less over-pessimistic than DRO, both under rank-preserving rewards and through relative concentrability.

The rest of the paper introduces the model, develops the promptwise theory and DRRO-GRPO algorithm, reports the experiments, and then compares DRO and DRRO theoretically. The proofs and further details are deferred to the appendix.

2 RLHF as Ex-Ante Regret Robustness

This section formalizes the RLHF decision problem. We fix notation for prompts, policies, proxy rewards, and latent human preferences, then show how a Wasserstein ambiguity set over reward distributions reduces to the promptwise mean-reward ambiguity set solved in Section 3.

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be the prompt space and let 𝒟\mathcal{D} be the prompt distribution used for training and deployment evaluation. For the current prompt, let 𝒴\mathcal{Y} denote the set of complete responses. This set is astronomically large but conceptually finite after fixing a vocabulary and maximum generation length; the theory uses this finite simplex view, while the algorithm only samples completions. A policy πθ(⋅∣x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) assigns probabilities to complete responses, π0\pi_{0} denotes the frozen reference policy, and π¯\bar{\pi} denotes the rollout policy used during a policy-gradient update.

Each user uu has a latent preference reward ru⋆​(x,y)r^{\star}_{u}(x,y). The user population 𝒬\mathcal{Q} induces a distribution 𝒫⋆\mathcal{P}^{\star} over reward functions, while the learned reward model r^​(x,y)\hat{r}(x,y) is only a proxy for this population signal. For any distribution PP over reward functions, define

JP(π)≔𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼π(⋅∣x),R∼P[R(x,y)].J_{P}(\pi)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\ y\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x),\ R\sim P}[R(x,y)]. (2.1)

For the true population law, J𝒫⋆(π)=𝔼u∼𝒬,x∼𝒟,y∼π(⋅∣x)[ru⋆(x,y)]J_{\mathcal{P}^{\star}}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{u\sim\mathcal{Q},\ x\sim\mathcal{D},\ y\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x)}[r^{\star}_{u}(x,y)]. If P=δrP=\delta_{r} is a point mass on reward function rr, write Jr(π)≔𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼π(⋅∣x)[r(x,y)]J_{r}(\pi)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\ y\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x)}[r(x,y)]. By linearity, only the certainty-equivalent reward r¯P​(x,y)≔𝔼R∼P​[R⁡(x,y)]\bar{r}_{P}(x,y)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{R\sim P}[R(x,y)] matters: JP​(π)=Jr¯P​(π)J_{P}(\pi)=J_{\bar{r}_{P}}(\pi). We set r⋆≔r¯𝒫⋆r^{\star}\coloneqq\bar{r}_{\mathcal{P}^{\star}} and let Π\Pi denote the policy class considered by the robust decision problem.

Nominal RLHF maximizes Jr^​(π)J_{\hat{r}}(\pi), often with KL or clipping controls inherited from PPO-style training (Schulman et al., 2017). Our algorithms do not add an explicit KL penalty to the policy objective: the robust correction changes the reward signal rather than merely restricting optimization of the same proxy. KL reappears only as a drift statistic for calibrating the dynamic ambiguity budget; Appendix C gives more detail.

The closed-form theory is promptwise. Fix xx and enumerate its complete responses as y1,…,yny_{1},\ldots,y_{n}. Write πi​(x)≔π⁡(yi∣x)\pi_{i}(x)\coloneqq\pi(y_{i}\mid x) and βi​(x)≔β⁡(yi∣x)\beta_{i}(x)\coloneqq\beta(y_{i}\mid x), so π⁡(x),β⁡(x)∈Δn\pi(x),\beta(x)\in\Delta_{n}, where Δn≔{ζ∈ℝ+n:∑iζi=1}\Delta_{n}\coloneqq\{\zeta\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}:\sum_{i}\zeta_{i}=1\}. For any reward function rr, define ri​(x)≔r⁡(x,yi)r_{i}(x)\coloneqq r(x,y_{i}) and r⁡(x)≔(r1​(x),…,rn​(x))∈ℝnr(x)\coloneqq(r_{1}(x),\ldots,r_{n}(x))\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. Similarly, r^​(x)∈ℝn\hat{r}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{n} denotes the promptwise proxy-reward vector.

Let P0≔δr^P_{0}\coloneqq\delta_{\hat{r}} be the nominal point mass on the learned reward model. For p,q≥1p,q\geq 1, define the promptwise ground metric

dp​(μ,ν)≔‖μ−ν‖p,d_{p}(\mu,\nu)\coloneqq\left\lVert\mu-\nu\right\rVert_{p},

and let 𝒲q,dp\mathcal{W}_{q,d_{p}} be the qq-Wasserstein distance induced by the ground metric dpd_{p}:

𝒲q,dp​(P,Q,x)\displaystyle\mathcal{W}_{q,d_{p}}(P,Q;x) ≔(infγ∈Γ⁡(P,Q)𝔼γ​[dp​(R⁡(x),R~​(x))q])1/q,\displaystyle\coloneqq\left(\inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma(P,Q)}\mathbb{E}_{\gamma}\!\left[d_{p}(R(x),\widetilde{R}(x))^{q}\right]\right)^{1/q}, (2.2)

where Γ⁡(P,Q)\Gamma(P,Q) is the set of couplings of PP and QQ. The mean-reward reduction below holds for all p,q≥1p,q\geq 1, so the robust model can be stated for any norm-induced transport geometry. For fixed p,qp,q, define the ambiguity set

𝒰δ​(P0)≔{P:𝒲q,dp​(P,P0,x)≤δ​for every ​x∈𝒳}.\mathcal{U}_{\delta}(P_{0})\coloneqq\left\{P:\ \mathcal{W}_{q,d_{p}}(P,P_{0};x)\leq\delta\ \text{for every }x\in\mathcal{X}\right\}. (2.3)

Here δ\delta is the scalar ambiguity budget, not the Dirac delta in P0=δr^P_{0}=\delta_{\hat{r}}. The algorithmic section later specializes to p=1p=1, because that geometry gives the coordinate-local correction needed for sampled completions; see Sections 4.5 and 4.5.

The decision is ex ante: the learner chooses one policy before knowing which plausible reward distribution will govern deployment. The DRRO problem is

minπ∈Π⁡maxP∈𝒰δ​(P0)​[maxβ∈Π⁡JP​(β)−JP​(π)],\min_{\pi\in\Pi}\ \max_{P\in\mathcal{U}_{\delta}(P_{0})}\left[\max_{\beta\in\Pi}J_{P}(\beta)-J_{P}(\pi)\right], (2.4)

where β\beta is the hindsight policy that would be selected if PP were known. This benchmark is the key distinction: DRRO compares the chosen policy with the best policy in the same plausible world, whereas DRO evaluates absolute worst-case value.

Proposition 2.1 (Mean-reward reduction).

For any policy π\pi and any distribution PP over reward functions, define the mean reward

r¯P​(x,y):=𝔼R∼P​[R⁡(x,y)].\bar{r}_{P}(x,y):=\mathbb{E}_{R\sim P}[R(x,y)].

Then

JP​(π)=Jr¯P​(π).J_{P}(\pi)=J_{\bar{r}_{P}}(\pi).

Consequently, the ex-ante DRRO objective depends on PP only through the induced mean-reward set.

Corollary 2.2 (Promptwise Wasserstein ambiguity induces mean-reward ambiguity).

Fix a prompt xx and view each reward function through its vector

R⁡(x)≔(R⁡(x,y1),…,R⁡(x,yn)).R(x)\coloneqq(R(x,y_{1}),\ldots,R(x,y_{n})).

For any p,q≥1p,q\geq 1, any candidate mean-reward vector s⁡(x)s(x), and any budget δ≥0\delta\geq 0,

∃P​such that​𝔼R∼P​[R⁡(x)]=s⁡(x)​and​𝒲q,dp​(P,P0,x)≤δ\displaystyle\exists P\ \text{such that}\ \mathbb{E}_{R\sim P}[R(x)]=s(x)\ \text{and}\ \mathcal{W}_{q,d_{p}}(P,P_{0};x)\leq\delta
⟺‖s(x)−𝔼R∼P0[R(x)]‖p≤δ.\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\left\|s(x)-\mathbb{E}_{R\sim P_{0}}[R(x)]\right\|_{p}\leq\delta.

Propositions 2.1 and 2.2 justify replacing reward-distribution ambiguity by deterministic ambiguity over mean rewards. With P0=δr^P_{0}=\delta_{\hat{r}} and transport cost dpd_{p}, the induced fixed-prompt set is

ℳδ,p​(r^​(x))≔{s⁡(x)∈ℝn:‖s⁡(x)−r^​(x)‖p≤δ}.\mathcal{M}_{\delta,p}(\hat{r}(x))\coloneqq\left\{s(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\ \left\lVert s(x)-\hat{r}(x)\right\rVert_{p}\leq\delta\right\}. (2.5)

Thus δ\delta controls the allowable promptwise reward perturbation: small δ\delta trusts the proxy, while large δ\delta asks the policy to hedge against reward-model extrapolation error.

3 Closed-Form Promptwise Analysis

We now isolate the core promptwise optimization problem and solve it exactly. The first step is to justify why this reduction is not merely a heuristic convenience. If the policy class is rich enough to realize arbitrary promptwise response distributions, then the global ex-ante DRRO problem factorizes into independent promptwise problems for any fixed norm parameter pp.

Proposition 3.1 (Promptwise decomposition).

Assume the policy class is the full product space Πfull≔Δn𝒳\Pi_{\mathrm{full}}\coloneqq\Delta_{n}^{\mathcal{X}}, suppressing the harmless prompt-dependence of nn in the notation. Fix 1≤p≤∞1\leq p\leq\infty and define

ℳδ,p𝒳​(r^)≔{s:s⁡(x)∈ℳδ,p​(r^​(x))​ for every ​x∈𝒳},\mathcal{M}_{\delta,p}^{\mathcal{X}}(\hat{r})\coloneqq\left\{s:\ s(x)\in\mathcal{M}_{\delta,p}(\hat{r}(x))\text{ for every }x\in\mathcal{X}\right\},

and, for ζ∈Δn\zeta\in\Delta_{n}, write

Regx⁡(ζ,s⁡(x))≔maxβ∈Δn⁡⟨β−ζ,s⁡(x)⟩.\Reg_{x}(\zeta,s(x))\coloneqq\max_{\beta\in\Delta_{n}}\left\langle\beta-\zeta,s(x)\right\rangle.

Then, for any fixed policy π\pi, an optimal global adversary is exactly a direct product of optimal promptwise adversaries:

s⋆​(x)∈arg​maxs⁡(x)∈ℳδ,p​(r^​(x))⁡Regx⁡(π⁡(x),s⁡(x))for ​𝒟​-a.e. ​x,s^{\star}(x)\in\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{s(x)\in\mathcal{M}_{\delta,p}(\hat{r}(x))}\Reg_{x}(\pi(x),s(x))\quad\text{for }\mathcal{D}\text{-a.e. }x,

and conversely any such direct product is globally optimal. Moreover, a policy π⋆\pi^{\star} is globally optimal if and only if it is a direct product of optimal promptwise policies:

π⋆​(x)∈arg​minζ∈Δn⁡maxs⁡(x)∈ℳδ,p​(r^​(x))⁡Regx⁡(ζ,s⁡(x))for ​𝒟​-a.e. ​x.\pi^{\star}(x)\in\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{\zeta\in\Delta_{n}}\max_{s(x)\in\mathcal{M}_{\delta,p}(\hat{r}(x))}\Reg_{x}(\zeta,s(x))\quad\text{for }\mathcal{D}\text{-a.e. }x.
Remark 3.2 (Approximate decomposition for realizable LLM policies).

The proposition is stated for the full product policy class, where the learner may choose a separate distribution for every prompt. A real LLM is not that flexible: the same parameters shape responses across many prompts, and a gradient update must fit all promptwise signals through one shared neural policy. Still, the decomposition is the right local picture when the model class is expressive on the prompts being trained. The promptwise DRRO solution says what each prompt would like the policy to do if it could move freely; the implemented policy-gradient algorithm then asks the LLM to approximate those directions as well as its parameterization allows. In this sense, realizability error enters as a coupling effect across prompts, not as a change in the robust objective itself.

The proposition says that promptwise analysis is exact for an expressive policy class and therefore a useful structural guide for large language models. The rest of this section fixes a prompt and studies the resulting simplex problem. This is where the main theoretical intuition becomes visible: the adversary has a remarkably explicit dual-norm target, and under the ℓ1\ell_{1} geometry used later by the algorithm, the optimizer becomes a water-filling allocation that protects responses whose proxy rewards are high but whose current policy coverage is too low.

3.1 Fixed-Prompt Simplex Model

Fix a prompt xx and enumerate its possible complete responses as y1,…,yny_{1},\ldots,y_{n}. Write

π=(π1,…,πn)∈Δn,πi=π⁡(yi∣x),\pi=(\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{n})\in\Delta_{n},\qquad\pi_{i}=\pi(y_{i}\mid x),

and define the promptwise proxy-reward vector

r^=(r^1,…,r^n),r^i=r^​(x,yi).\hat{r}=(\hat{r}_{1},\ldots,\hat{r}_{n}),\qquad\hat{r}_{i}=\hat{r}(x,y_{i}).

For a norm parameter 1≤p≤∞1\leq p\leq\infty and a perturbation Δ∈ℝn\Delta\in\mathbb{R}^{n} with ‖Δ‖p≤δ\left\lVert\Delta\right\rVert_{p}\leq\delta, let the plausible reward vector be

s=r^+Δ.s=\hat{r}+\Delta.

The promptwise regret of policy π\pi under ss is

Reg⁡(π,s):=maxβ∈Δn⁡⟨β−π,s⟩.\Reg(\pi,s):=\max_{\beta\in\Delta_{n}}\left\langle\beta-\pi,s\right\rangle.

Define the fixed-policy worst-case regret

Ψp​(π,r^)≔max‖Δ‖p≤δ⁡Reg⁡(π,r^+Δ).\Psi_{p}(\pi;\hat{r})\coloneqq\max_{\left\lVert\Delta\right\rVert_{p}\leq\delta}\Reg(\pi,\hat{r}+\Delta). (3.1)

The ℓ1\ell_{1} specialization used by the algorithm is the promptwise problem

minπ∈Δn⁡max‖Δ‖1≤δ​Reg⁡(π,r^+Δ).\min_{\pi\in\Delta_{n}}\ \max_{\left\lVert\Delta\right\rVert_{1}\leq\delta}\Reg(\pi,\hat{r}+\Delta). (3.2)
Proposition 3.3 (Inner adversary for a fixed policy).

Let 1≤p≤∞1\leq p\leq\infty, and let p∗p^{\ast} be the dual exponent, with p∗=∞p^{\ast}=\infty when p=1p=1 and p∗=1p^{\ast}=1 when p=∞p=\infty. For every π∈Δn\pi\in\Delta_{n},

Ψp​(π,r^)=max1≤i≤n⁡{r^i−⟨π,r^⟩+δ​‖ei−π‖p∗}.\Psi_{p}(\pi;\hat{r})=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\left\{\hat{r}_{i}-\left\langle\pi,\hat{r}\right\rangle+\delta\left\lVert e_{i}-\pi\right\rVert_{p^{\ast}}\right\}. (3.3)

Let kk be any maximizer in (3.3). If 1<p<∞1<p<\infty and ek≠πe_{k}\neq\pi, one optimal perturbation is

Δj⋆=δsgn⁡((ek−π)j)​|(ek−π)j|p∗−1‖ek−π‖p∗p∗−1,j=1,…,n.\Delta_{j}^{\star}=\delta\,\frac{\operatorname{sgn}((e_{k}-\pi)_{j})\left|(e_{k}-\pi)_{j}\right|^{p^{\ast}-1}}{\left\lVert e_{k}-\pi\right\rVert_{p^{\ast}}^{p^{\ast}-1}},\qquad j=1,\ldots,n. (3.4)

If p=∞p=\infty, one may instead take Δj⋆=δ​sgn⁡((ek−π)j)\Delta_{j}^{\star}=\delta\,\operatorname{sgn}((e_{k}-\pi)_{j}), with any value in [−δ,δ][-\delta,\delta] on zero coordinates. Specifically, when p=1p=1, the value reduces to

max‖Δ‖1≤δ⁡Reg⁡(π,r^+Δ)=δ+max1≤i≤n⁡(r^i−δ​πi)−⟨π,r^⟩.\max_{\left\lVert\Delta\right\rVert_{1}\leq\delta}\Reg(\pi,\hat{r}+\Delta)=\delta+\max_{1\leq i\leq n}(\hat{r}_{i}-\delta\pi_{i})-\left\langle\pi,\hat{r}\right\rangle. (3.5)

The inner adversary can then be chosen to place its entire budget on a single response:

Δ⋆=δ​ek,k∈arg​max1≤i≤n⁡{r^i−δ​πi}.\Delta^{\star}=\delta e_{k},\qquad k\in\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{1\leq i\leq n}\{\hat{r}_{i}-\delta\pi_{i}\}.

Proposition 3.3 identifies the adversarial target through the dual norm ‖ei−π‖p∗\left\lVert e_{i}-\pi\right\rVert_{p^{\ast}}. For p=1p=1, this target simplifies to the index r^i−δ​πi\hat{r}_{i}-\delta\pi_{i}: responses that have both high proxy reward and insufficient policy mass. That simple index becomes the backbone of the RLHF algorithm developed later.

Proposition 3.4 (General ℓp\ell_{p} epigraph form).

Fix 1<p≤∞1<p\leq\infty, and let p∗p^{\ast} be the dual exponent. The minimizers of the promptwise ℓp\ell_{p}-DRRO problem

minπ∈Δn⁡Ψp​(π,r^)\min_{\pi\in\Delta_{n}}\Psi_{p}(\pi;\hat{r})

are exactly the first components of the solutions to the convex epigraph problem

minπ∈Δn,t∈ℝ\displaystyle\min_{\pi\in\Delta_{n},\ t\in\mathbb{R}} t−⟨π,r^⟩\displaystyle t-\left\langle\pi,\hat{r}\right\rangle (3.6)
subject to\displaystyle\text{subject to} t≥r^i+δ‖ei−π‖p∗,i=1,…,n.\displaystyle t\geq\hat{r}_{i}+\delta\left\lVert e_{i}-\pi\right\rVert_{p^{\ast}},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.

Proposition 3.4 gives an exact finite-dimensional convex representation for every p>1p>1. The special case p=1p=1 is sharper: the epigraph constraints become linear after using ‖ei−π‖∞=1−πi\left\lVert e_{i}-\pi\right\rVert_{\infty}=1-\pi_{i}, and the optimizer can be written in the water-filling form below.

3.2 Water-Filling Structure of Promptwise Optimizer

Assume without loss of generality that the responses are labeled so that

r^1≥r^2≥⋯≥r^n.\hat{r}_{1}\geq\hat{r}_{2}\geq\cdots\geq\hat{r}_{n}. (3.7)

Define the promptwise robust utility

Fδ​(π,r^):=⟨π,r^⟩−max1≤i≤n⁡(r^i−δ​πi),F_{\delta}(\pi;\hat{r}):=\left\langle\pi,\hat{r}\right\rangle-\max_{1\leq i\leq n}(\hat{r}_{i}-\delta\pi_{i}), (3.8)

which differs from the worst-case regret in (3.5) only by the additive constant δ\delta.

Two structural facts already point toward a water-filling solution. First, the robust correction depends on the uncovered rewards r^i−δ​πi\hat{r}_{i}-\delta\pi_{i}, so moving mass toward a response is useful only until that uncovered level has been pushed down to the common threshold. Second, once the rewards are ordered as in (3.7), there is no reason to hedge a lower-scoring response before the higher-scoring ones have been brought down to the same uncovered level. The optimal policy therefore has to equalize a subset of uncovered rewards and leave any residual mass on the best response.

Theorem 3.5 (Water-filling with leftover mass).

Assume (3.7) and δ>0\delta>0. Let t0t_{0} be the unique solution to

∑i=1n(r^i−t)+=δ.\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\hat{r}_{i}-t)_{+}=\delta. (3.9)

Define

t⋆:=inf{t≥t0:∑i:r^i>t(r^1−r^i)≤δ}.t^{\star}:=\inf\left\{t\geq t_{0}:\ \sum_{i:\hat{r}_{i}>t}(\hat{r}_{1}-\hat{r}_{i})\leq\delta\right\}.

Then an optimal solution to (3.2) is

πi⋆\displaystyle\pi_{i}^{\star} =(r^i−t⋆)+δ,\displaystyle=\frac{(\hat{r}_{i}-t^{\star})_{+}}{\delta}, i=2,…,n,\displaystyle i=2,\ldots,n, (3.10)
π1⋆\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{\star} =1−1δ​∑i=2n(r^i−t⋆)+.\displaystyle=1-\frac{1}{\delta}\sum_{i=2}^{n}(\hat{r}_{i}-t^{\star})_{+}.

Theorem 3.5 is a genuine water-filling rule, but with an RLHF-specific twist. All nonmaximal responses receive precisely the excess of their proxy reward above the optimal threshold t⋆t^{\star}, while the remaining probability mass is assigned to the best response. When δ\delta is small, the threshold is high and the policy stays concentrated. As δ\delta grows, new responses enter the hedge. Once δ\delta is large enough that t⋆=t0<r^nt^{\star}=t_{0}<\hat{r}_{n}, every response receives positive mass and the policy approaches the uniform distribution. Appendix E contains the proof. For the main text, the important point is qualitative: the ambiguity budget lowers a threshold through the ordered proxy rewards, and probability is assigned only to responses whose uncovered rewards remain above that threshold.

3.3 Interpreting Water-Filling Policy

The water-filling theorem is useful not only because it is explicit, but also because it explains how the robustness budget changes the policy qualitatively. The policy does not flatten all responses equally. It first hedges against nearby competitors, then gradually widens support as the ambiguity budget grows, and it always keeps any residual probability mass on the top-ranked response.

Figure 2 makes the mechanics of the optimizer visible. Small ambiguity budgets trust the proxy and therefore keep most probability on the best response, with only the nearest competitor receiving hedge mass. As δ\delta increases, the threshold t⋆t^{\star} falls and further responses enter the active support one by one. What matters is not their absolute rank alone, but whether their uncovered rewards still sit above the current water level.

Sanity checks.

The limiting regimes line up with the intended interpretation of δ\delta. As δ↓0\delta\downarrow 0, the cost of hedging dominates and the optimizer converges to the proxy-greedy policy e1e_{1}. At the other extreme, once δ>∑i=1n(r^i−r^n)\delta>\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\hat{r}_{i}-\hat{r}_{n}) every response is active, so t⋆=t0=r^¯−δ/nt^{\star}=t_{0}=\bar{\hat{r}}-\delta/n with r^¯=1n​∑i=1nr^i\bar{\hat{r}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{r}_{i}, and the water-filling rule simplifies to

πi⋆=1n+r^i−r^¯δ,i=1,…,n.\pi_{i}^{\star}=\frac{1}{n}+\frac{\hat{r}_{i}-\bar{\hat{r}}}{\delta},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.

Hence π⋆\pi^{\star} approaches the uniform distribution as δ→∞\delta\to\infty. DRRO therefore interpolates continuously between proxy-greedy optimization and complete hedging, which is exactly the behavior one would want from an ambiguity budget.

4 Algorithm for RLHF

The exact promptwise solution from Section 3 tells us what a regret-robust policy should look like once a prompt has been reduced to a finite simplex. RLHF training, however, never gets to move probability mass on that simplex directly. What it actually sees are sampled completions from a language model, and what it actually updates are model parameters.

Throughout this section we specialize to the ℓ1\ell_{1} ambiguity geometry, whose locality is what makes the sampled bonus implementable; Sections 4.5 and 4.5 explains this choice.

Those two viewpoints are close enough to guide the algorithm, but different enough to create real work. For a fixed prompt, the response space is astronomically large, so the adversarial coordinate from Proposition 3.3 is hidden from us and can only be glimpsed through a small sampled group. And even if the promptwise optimizer were available in closed form, it would still not produce a usable LLM update, because the policy is an LLM parameterized by θ\theta and the trainable object is θ\theta, not the full vector π(⋅∣x)\pi(\cdot\mid x). The way forward is therefore to rewrite the robust objective as a policy-gradient recipe, understand what bonus the exact theory implies, and then relax that bonus until it can be estimated reliably from grouped rollouts.

4.1 From Promptwise Simplex to Policy Gradients

The theory above treats a complete response as one action. This is the right abstraction for the robust objective: the reward model scores completed responses, GRPO groups completed responses, and the policy-gradient update uses the sequence log-probability supplied by the language model. Thus we can work at the completion level without losing compatibility with standard LLM post-training.

For a fixed prompt xx, enumerate the candidate complete responses as y1,…,yny_{1},\ldots,y_{n} and write

πθ,i=πθ​(yi∣x),r^i=r^​(x,yi).\pi_{\theta,i}=\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x),\qquad\hat{r}_{i}=\hat{r}(x,y_{i}).

The nominal promptwise RLHF target is simply the expected proxy reward

⟨πθ(⋅∣x),r^(x)⟩=∑i=1nπθ,ir^i.\left\langle\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x),\hat{r}(x)\right\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\pi_{\theta,i}\hat{r}_{i}.

Differentiating this nominal target with respect to θ\theta gives

∇θ⟨πθ(⋅∣x),r^(x)⟩=∑i=1nr^i∇θπθ(yi∣x)=∑i=1nπθ(yi∣x)r^i∇θlogπθ(yi∣x).\nabla_{\theta}\left\langle\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x),\hat{r}(x)\right\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{r}_{i}\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x)\hat{r}_{i}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x).

Equivalently,

∇θ⟨πθ(⋅∣x),r^(x)⟩=𝔼y∼πθ(⋅∣x)[r^(x,y)∇θlogπθ(y∣x)].\nabla_{\theta}\left\langle\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x),\hat{r}(x)\right\rangle=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}\big[\hat{r}(x,y)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\big].

Hence, if y(1),…,y(K)∼πθ(⋅∣x)y^{(1)},\ldots,y^{(K)}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) are sampled on policy, then

g^θnom​(x):=1K​∑k=1Kr^​(x,y(k))​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y(k)∣x)\widehat{g}_{\theta}^{\mathrm{nom}}(x):=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\hat{r}(x,y^{(k)})\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y^{(k)}\mid x)

is an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator of the nominal policy gradient above. When the samples instead come from a frozen rollout policy π¯=πθold\bar{\pi}=\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}, standard importance sampling yields the detached estimator

g^θ,π¯nom(x):=1K∑k=1Kρθ(x,y(k))r^(x,y(k))∇θlogπθ(y(k)∣x),y(k)∼π¯(⋅∣x),\widehat{g}_{\theta,\bar{\pi}}^{\mathrm{nom}}(x):=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\rho_{\theta}(x,y^{(k)})\,\hat{r}(x,y^{(k)})\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y^{(k)}\mid x),\qquad y^{(k)}\sim\bar{\pi}(\cdot\mid x),

where ρθ​(x,y)=πθ​(y∣x)/π¯​(y∣x)\rho_{\theta}(x,y)=\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)/\bar{\pi}(y\mid x).

Now fix a rollout policy π¯=πθold\bar{\pi}=\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}} and let r~π¯​(x,y)\widetilde{r}_{\bar{\pi}}(x,y) be any promptwise reward signal computed from that frozen policy. This setup is deliberately broad: standard RLHF corresponds to r~π¯=r^\widetilde{r}_{\bar{\pi}}=\hat{r}, while our DRRO variants will use shaped rewards derived from the robust theory. Define

J~π¯(θ):=𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼πθ(⋅∣x)[r~π¯(x,y)].\widetilde{J}_{\bar{\pi}}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\ y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}[\widetilde{r}_{\bar{\pi}}(x,y)].

Because the reward is detached during the policy update, the score-function identity gives

∇θJ~π¯(θ)=𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼πθ(⋅∣x)[r~π¯(x,y)∇θlogπθ(y∣x)].\nabla_{\theta}\widetilde{J}_{\bar{\pi}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\ y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}\big[\widetilde{r}_{\bar{\pi}}(x,y)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\big].

Equivalently, if the responses were generated from π¯\bar{\pi}, then

J~π¯(θ)=𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼π¯(⋅∣x)[ρθ(x,y)r~π¯(x,y)],ρθ(x,y):=πθ​(y∣x)π¯​(y∣x).\widetilde{J}_{\bar{\pi}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\ y\sim\bar{\pi}(\cdot\mid x)}\Big[\rho_{\theta}(x,y)\,\widetilde{r}_{\bar{\pi}}(x,y)\Big],\qquad\rho_{\theta}(x,y):=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)}{\bar{\pi}(y\mid x)}.

This is the starting point for GRPO-style clipped surrogates: one samples groups of responses from a frozen rollout policy, computes detached rewards or advantages on those responses, and then performs several stable gradient steps on θ\theta. The two algorithm boxes in this section should therefore be read as policy-gradient procedures with an explicit outer rollout/update loop.

4.2 GRPO as Standard Grouped RLHF Backbone

Before inserting any robust correction, it helps to recall the grouped RLHF template that practitioners already use. The importance-sampling estimator above is the original recipe: estimate the gradient of the nominal promptwise target ⟨πθ(⋅∣x),r^(x)⟩\left\langle\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x),\hat{r}(x)\right\rangle from sampled completions and then ascend along that estimate. Following Shao et al. (2024), GRPO stabilizes that recipe by grouping completions promptwise, replacing raw rewards by normalized within-group advantages, and clipping the importance ratio inside the policy update. Concretely, for each prompt xx we sample a group of completions

y(1),…,y(G)∼π¯(⋅∣x),y^{(1)},\ldots,y^{(G)}\sim\bar{\pi}(\cdot\mid x),

evaluate them with the proxy reward model,

r^(k)=r^(x,y(k)),k=1,…,G,\widehat{r}^{(k)}=\hat{r}(x,y^{(k)}),\qquad k=1,\ldots,G,

and normalize the groupwise rewards into relative advantages

r¯\displaystyle\bar{r} :=1G∑ℓ=1Gr^(ℓ),sr2:=1G∑ℓ=1G(r^(ℓ)−r¯)2,\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{\ell=1}^{G}\widehat{r}^{(\ell)},\qquad s_{r}^{2}:=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{\ell=1}^{G}(\widehat{r}^{(\ell)}-\bar{r})^{2}, (4.1)
AGRPO(k)\displaystyle A_{\mathrm{GRPO}}^{(k)} :=r^(k)−r¯sr+εadv.\displaystyle:=\frac{\widehat{r}^{(k)}-\bar{r}}{s_{r}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{adv}}}.

The completion-level GRPO surrogate is then

ℒGRPO​(θ,π¯)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\theta;\bar{\pi}) :=𝔼⁡[1G​∑k=1Gℓθ(k)],\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{k=1}^{G}\ell_{\theta}^{(k)}\right], (4.2)
ℓθ(k)\displaystyle\ell_{\theta}^{(k)} :=min⁡{ρθ(k)​AGRPO(k),cθ(k)​AGRPO(k)}.\displaystyle:=\min\!\left\{\rho_{\theta}^{(k)}A_{\mathrm{GRPO}}^{(k)},c_{\theta}^{(k)}A_{\mathrm{GRPO}}^{(k)}\right\}.

where the expectation is over x∼𝒟x\sim\mathcal{D} and y(1),…,y(G)∼π¯(⋅∣x)y^{(1)},\ldots,y^{(G)}\sim\bar{\pi}(\cdot\mid x), and

ρθ(k)\displaystyle\rho_{\theta}^{(k)} :=πθ​(y(k)∣x)π¯​(y(k)∣x),\displaystyle:=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y^{(k)}\mid x)}{\bar{\pi}(y^{(k)}\mid x)},
cθ(k)\displaystyle c_{\theta}^{(k)} :=clip⁡(ρθ(k),1−εclip,1+εclip).\displaystyle:=\operatorname{clip}\bigl(\rho_{\theta}^{(k)},1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}},1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}\bigr).

This is the baseline recipe to which our DRRO corrections will be compared. Everything that follows keeps the grouped rollout, importance-ratio, and clipped policy-gradient backbone of (4.2); only the reward signal inside the group changes. In particular, we do not add any explicit KL penalty term to the policy objective.

4.3 Soft-Max Relaxation and Sampled Estimation

The exact promptwise DRRO objective contains the maximum maxi⁡(r^i−δ​πi)\max_{i}(\hat{r}_{i}-\delta\pi_{i}). On the finite simplex this term is perfectly well defined, but in RLHF it is not directly observable: the response space is too large to enumerate, and a rollout group shows only a small random subset of possible completions. Estimating the maximum by taking the largest value inside the sampled group is therefore not faithful to the target in general, because the response attaining the true maximum over the hidden simplex may simply not have been sampled.

We therefore replace the exact maximum by a smooth log-sum-exp relaxation. The point of this relaxation is not cosmetic: it converts the adversarial correction into an expectation under a soft adversarial distribution, which can be approximated from sampled completions. For a fixed prompt, define

Fδ,τ​(π,r^)\displaystyle F_{\delta,\tau}(\pi;\hat{r}) :=⟨π,r^⟩−τ​log⁡Zτ​(π,r^),\displaystyle:=\left\langle\pi,\hat{r}\right\rangle-\tau\log Z_{\tau}(\pi;\hat{r}), (4.3)
Zτ​(π,r^)\displaystyle Z_{\tau}(\pi;\hat{r}) :=∑i=1nexp(r^i−δ​πiτ),τ>0.\displaystyle:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\exp\!\left(\frac{\hat{r}_{i}-\delta\pi_{i}}{\tau}\right),\qquad\tau>0.

This is the smooth target we will optimize through sampled completions.

Proposition 4.1 (Soft-max approximation error).

For every promptwise policy π∈Δn\pi\in\Delta_{n} and proxy-reward vector r^∈ℝn\hat{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{n},

Fδ,τ​(π,r^)≤Fδ​(π,r^)≤Fδ,τ​(π,r^)+τ​log⁡n.F_{\delta,\tau}(\pi;\hat{r})\leq F_{\delta}(\pi;\hat{r})\leq F_{\delta,\tau}(\pi;\hat{r})+\tau\log n. (4.4)

Thus smaller temperature means a smaller approximation gap to the exact promptwise objective. The price is that the induced adversarial distribution becomes more concentrated, so approximating that distribution from samples becomes harder. This is the central tradeoff in the soft formulation: low temperature reduces optimization bias, but it also makes the sampled approximation of the extra regret term less forgiving.

The smooth objective has an exact gradient that again takes the form of reward shaping.

Proposition 4.2 (Gradient of the soft DRRO objective).

Fix a prompt xx and treat δ\delta as fixed during the policy-gradient step. Define

πθ,i:=πθ​(yi∣x),r^i:=r^​(x,yi),σθ,x​(yi):=exp⁡((r^i−δ​πθ,i)/τ)∑j=1nexp⁡((r^j−δ​πθ,j)/τ).\pi_{\theta,i}:=\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x),\qquad\hat{r}_{i}:=\hat{r}(x,y_{i}),\qquad\sigma_{\theta,x}(y_{i}):=\frac{\exp((\hat{r}_{i}-\delta\pi_{\theta,i})/\tau)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\exp((\hat{r}_{j}-\delta\pi_{\theta,j})/\tau)}.

Then

gθsoft​(x)\displaystyle g_{\theta}^{\mathrm{soft}}(x) :=∇θFδ,τ(πθ(⋅∣x);r^(x)),\displaystyle:=\nabla_{\theta}F_{\delta,\tau}(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x);\hat{r}(x)), (4.5)
gθsoft​(x)\displaystyle g_{\theta}^{\mathrm{soft}}(x) =∑i=1nπθ​(yi∣x)​Risoft​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(yi∣x),\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x)R_{i}^{\mathrm{soft}}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x),
Risoft\displaystyle R_{i}^{\mathrm{soft}} :=r^i+Bisoft,\displaystyle:=\hat{r}_{i}+{\color[rgb]{0,0,0.7}B_{i}^{\mathrm{soft}}},
Bisoft\displaystyle B_{i}^{\mathrm{soft}} :=δ​σθ,x​(yi).\displaystyle:=\delta\,\sigma_{\theta,x}(y_{i}).

Equation (4.5) has the same policy-gradient form as nominal RLHF, except that the proxy reward is augmented by the robust bonus BisoftB_{i}^{\mathrm{soft}}. This bonus is proportional to the soft adversarial probability mass σθ,x​(yi)\sigma_{\theta,x}(y_{i}). That representation is exactly what makes the correction estimable from partial samples: instead of identifying a single maximizer on the hidden simplex, we only need to approximate expectations under σθ,x\sigma_{\theta,x}.

To estimate these expectations, we use self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS). Suppose there is a proposal distribution q(⋅∣x)q(\cdot\mid x) over possible completions whose support covers the responses receiving nonnegligible soft-adversarial mass. For a fixed prompt and fixed budget δ\delta, define

aθ,x​(y):=exp⁡(r^​(x,y)−δ​πθ​(y∣x)τ),uq​(y):=aθ,x​(y)q⁡(y∣x).a_{\theta,x}(y):=\exp\!\left(\frac{\hat{r}(x,y)-\delta\,\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)}{\tau}\right),\qquad u_{q}(y):=\frac{a_{\theta,x}(y)}{q(y\mid x)}.

For samples y(1),…,y(K)∼q(⋅∣x)y^{(1)},\ldots,y^{(K)}\sim q(\cdot\mid x), set

u(k):=uq​(y(k)),w(k):=u(k)∑ℓ=1Ku(ℓ).u^{(k)}:=u_{q}(y^{(k)}),\qquad w^{(k)}:=\frac{u^{(k)}}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}u^{(\ell)}}. (4.6)

Then, for any bounded test function hh, the corresponding exact soft expectation can be written as

μh​(x):=∑i=1nσθ,x​(yi)​h​(yi)=𝔼y∼q(⋅∣x)[uq(y)h(y)]𝔼y∼q(⋅∣x)[uq(y)],\mu_{h}(x):=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{\theta,x}(y_{i})h(y_{i})=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{y\sim q(\cdot\mid x)}[u_{q}(y)h(y)]}{\mathbb{E}_{y\sim q(\cdot\mid x)}[u_{q}(y)]},

and the SNIS approximation is

μ^h,K​(x):=∑k=1Kw(k)​h​(y(k)).\widehat{\mu}_{h,K}(x):=\sum_{k=1}^{K}w^{(k)}h(y^{(k)}). (4.7)

The choice of proposal distribution is itself a substantive sampling question. In principle, qq could be any language-model proposal with adequate support. In this paper we use the rollout policy q=π¯q=\bar{\pi}, for a practical reason: the proposal distribution must itself be available during generation and log-probability computation, while memory is already tight in contemporary LLM inference. The rollout policy is already resident in the GRPO loop, so choosing q=π¯q=\bar{\pi} avoids storing or serving another proposal model while keeping the sampled estimator aligned with the policy update.

Finite-sample bias and concentration results for SNIS are classical; see, for example, Cardoso et al. (2022). For our grouped RLHF estimator, the following promptwise bound makes the dependence on the sample size KK explicit. In the statement, write u​(y)=uq​(y)u(y)=u_{q}(y). In the implementation below, one simply takes K=GK=G.

Proposition 4.3 (Finite-sample SNIS error).

Fix a prompt xx and a bounded test function hh. Suppose 0≤u⁡(y)≤Ux0\leq u(y)\leq U_{x} and |h⁡(y)|≤Hx|h(y)|\leq H_{x} for q(⋅∣x)q(\cdot\mid x)-almost every yy, and write

νx:=𝔼y∼q(⋅∣x)[u(y)]>0.\nu_{x}:=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim q(\cdot\mid x)}[u(y)]>0.

Then for every η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1), if

K≥2​Ux2νx2​log⁡4η,K\geq\frac{2U_{x}^{2}}{\nu_{x}^{2}}\log\frac{4}{\eta},

the estimator (4.7) satisfies

Pr⁡(EK)\displaystyle\Pr(E_{K}) ≥1−η,\displaystyle\geq 1-\eta, (4.8)
EK\displaystyle E_{K} :={|μ^h,K(x)−μh(x)|≤BK},\displaystyle:=\left\{\left|\widehat{\mu}_{h,K}(x)-\mu_{h}(x)\right|\leq B_{K}\right\},
BK\displaystyle B_{K} :=4​Ux​Hxνx​log⁡(4/η)2​K.\displaystyle:=\frac{4U_{x}H_{x}}{\nu_{x}}\sqrt{\frac{\log(4/\eta)}{2K}}.

The dependence on the temperature is now visible in two places. By Proposition 4.1, lower τ\tau makes the optimization target closer to the exact promptwise DRRO objective. But in (4.8), the constant UxU_{x} grows with the dynamic range of exp⁡((r^−δ​π)/τ)\exp((\hat{r}-\delta\pi)/\tau), so low temperature also increases the variance and decreases the effective sample size of the SNIS weights. The temperature therefore trades approximation bias against sampling stability.

For the rollout choice q=π¯q=\bar{\pi}, we evaluate the soft adversarial weights at the frozen rollout policy and write

r^(k):=r^​(x,y(k)),π¯(k):=π¯​(y(k)∣x).\widehat{r}^{(k)}:=\hat{r}(x,y^{(k)}),\qquad\bar{\pi}^{(k)}:=\bar{\pi}(y^{(k)}\mid x).

The soft reward-shaping gradient implied by (4.5) is then approximated by

g^θ​(x)=1G​∑k=1Gr~raw(k)​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y(k)∣x).\widehat{g}_{\theta}(x)=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{k=1}^{G}\widetilde{r}_{\mathrm{raw}}^{(k)}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y^{(k)}\mid x). (4.9)

Here the SNIS weights are computed from (4.6) with q=π¯q=\bar{\pi} and πθ\pi_{\theta} in aθ,xa_{\theta,x} frozen at π¯\bar{\pi}. Equivalently, one may define the soft DRRO-shaped rewards

r~raw(k)=r^(k)+δ​G​w(k)​π¯(k).\widetilde{r}_{\mathrm{raw}}^{(k)}=\widehat{r}^{(k)}+{\color[rgb]{0,0,0.7}\delta\,Gw^{(k)}\bar{\pi}^{(k)}}. (4.10)

Here the first term is again the ordinary proxy reward, while the second term is the robust bonus. The factor G​w(k)​π¯(k)Gw^{(k)}\bar{\pi}^{(k)} is the SNIS approximation to the soft adversarial mass assigned to response y(k)y^{(k)}.

The raw expression above is the conceptual soft-SNIS estimator. The practical implementation uses the group-normalized stabilization and scaled budget introduced in Section 4.4; this changes the numerical coordinate system of the sampled group, not the underlying soft DRRO target. In other words, we are now optimizing a grouped policy-gradient surrogate for the smooth promptwise target

Jδ,τsoft(π):=𝔼x∼𝒟[Fδ,τ(π(⋅∣x);r^(x,⋅))].J_{\delta,\tau}^{\mathrm{soft}}(\pi):=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\big[F_{\delta,\tau}(\pi(\cdot\mid x);\hat{r}(x,\cdot))\big].

4.4 Selection of Ambiguity δ\delta and Final Implemented Algorithm

At this point the mechanics are almost complete. The remaining design choice is how much ambiguity to grant the adversary at different stages of training.

Numerical stabilization.

Before selecting the budget, we first translate the raw sampled soft bonus in (4.10) into the coordinate system used by a finite rollout group. Raw completion probabilities π¯(k)\bar{\pi}^{(k)} can be extremely small, so the implementation uses group-normalized probabilities. Within each sampled group we set

π~(k)≔π¯(k)∑ℓ=1Gπ¯(ℓ).\widetilde{\pi}^{(k)}\coloneqq\frac{\bar{\pi}^{(k)}}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{G}\bar{\pi}^{(\ell)}}.

Under the heuristic scale π¯(k)≈1/n\bar{\pi}^{(k)}\approx 1/n, this normalization magnifies probabilities by about n/Gn/G. At the same time, the original Wasserstein budget δ\delta scales with the dimension nn of the conceptual reward vector, so the sampled implementation uses the scaled budget δ~≔(G/n)​δ\widetilde{\delta}\coloneqq(G/n)\delta. The practical soft DRRO bonus is

u~(k)\displaystyle\widetilde{u}^{(k)} ≔1π~(k)​exp⁡(r^(k)−δ~​π~(k)τ),\displaystyle\coloneqq\frac{1}{\widetilde{\pi}^{(k)}}\exp\!\left(\frac{\widehat{r}^{(k)}-\widetilde{\delta}\,\widetilde{\pi}^{(k)}}{\tau}\right), (4.11)
w~(k)\displaystyle\widetilde{w}^{(k)} ≔u~(k)∑ℓ=1Gu~(ℓ),\displaystyle\coloneqq\frac{\widetilde{u}^{(k)}}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{G}\widetilde{u}^{(\ell)}},
r~DRRO(k)\displaystyle\widetilde{r}_{\mathrm{DRRO}}^{(k)} ≔r^(k)+δ~​G​w~(k)​π~(k).\displaystyle\coloneqq\widehat{r}^{(k)}+{\color[rgb]{0,0,0.7}\widetilde{\delta}\,G\,\widetilde{w}^{(k)}\widetilde{\pi}^{(k)}}.

This is an implementation-level stabilization of the same soft DRRO target, not a different robust objective: the full-simplex theory still supplies the soft adversarial distribution, while the sampled update rescales the tiny rollout probabilities into a numerically usable group-level coordinate system. We then plug the group-normalized versions of r~DRRO(k)\widetilde{r}_{\mathrm{DRRO}}^{(k)} into the same clipped GRPO surrogate (4.2).

Dynamic ambiguity budget.

Keeping δ\delta fixed throughout training is unnecessarily rigid because reward-model error typically grows as the policy drifts away from the reference model. The Donsker–Varadhan variational formula gives a clean way to formalize that idea.

Proposition 4.4 (Donsker–Varadhan control of reward misspecification).

Fix a prompt xx and define

hx​(y):=|r^​(x,y)−r⋆​(x,y)|.h_{x}(y):=\big|\hat{r}(x,y)-r^{\star}(x,y)\big|.

Then for every λ>0\lambda>0,

𝔼y∼πθ(⋅∣x)[hx(y)]≤1λ[KL(πθ(⋅∣x)∥π0(⋅∣x))+log𝔼y∼π0(⋅∣x)[eλ​hx​(y)]].\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}[h_{x}(y)]\leq\frac{1}{\lambda}\left[\mathrm{KL}\big(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{0}(\cdot\mid x)\big)+\log\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot\mid x)}\!\big[e^{\lambda h_{x}(y)}\big]\right]. (4.12)

The formal inequality still contains the unknown log-moment term under π0\pi_{0}, but its three terms explain why KL drift is a sensible observable proxy for reward uncertainty. The left-hand side is an analogue of the promptwise ℓ1\ell_{1} error between the proxy reward and the certainty-equivalent true reward; the log-moment term can be treated as a baseline constant because it is evaluated under the fixed reference policy rather than the current policy; and the KL term is the observable policy-drift statistic that remains, with the tunable coefficient α\alpha in (4.13) playing the role of the multiplier 1/λ1/\lambda. In the implementation we therefore use the scaled sampled budget

δ~θ(x)=δ~0+αKL(π¯(⋅∣x)∥π0(⋅∣x)),\widetilde{\delta}_{\theta}(x)=\widetilde{\delta}_{0}+\alpha\,\mathrm{KL}\big(\bar{\pi}(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{0}(\cdot\mid x)\big), (4.13)

where δ~0≥0\widetilde{\delta}_{0}\geq 0 is a pilot-calibrated base budget and α>0\alpha>0 is a scaling coefficient. This KL quantity is used only to calibrate the ambiguity budget; it is not added as an explicit penalty to the policy objective.

In experiments, the KL term is estimated on sampled completions with the well-known k3k_{3} estimator of Schulman (2020): for z(k)=log⁡π0​(y(k)∣x)−log⁡π¯​(y(k)∣x)z^{(k)}=\log\pi_{0}(y^{(k)}\mid x)-\log\bar{\pi}(y^{(k)}\mid x), average exp⁡(z(k))−z(k)−1\exp(z^{(k)})-z^{(k)}-1 over the group. This statistic is nonnegative samplewise, has lower variance than the raw log-ratio estimator, and is differentiated through neither the budget nor the policy loss.

The calibration is deliberately pragmatic. We first draw a small pilot set of prompts, generate a modest number of responses from the initial policy, and score those responses with both the proxy reward model and a stronger held-out gold reward model. The empirical promptwise ℓ1\ell_{1} discrepancy between the two provides an initial guess for the unscaled budget and hence for δ~0\widetilde{\delta}_{0} after group normalization. After that, the remaining hyperparameters—notably α\alpha, τ\tau, the group size GG, and the clipping radius εclip\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}—are tuned on a standard held-out validation set evaluated by the stronger reward model.

The final implementation uses the soft bonus, the dynamic budget, and the unchanged GRPO backbone. Once the scaled promptwise budgets δ~b\widetilde{\delta}_{b} have been instantiated from (4.13), the only code-level modification inside the GRPO update is still the reward-shaping block.

4.5 Discussion

Two practical points deserve a final discussion: how much extra computation DRRO introduces on top of GRPO, and why the ℓ1\ell_{1} ambiguity set is the geometry that makes that extra computation tractable. Both points reinforce the same message of this section, namely that the robust correction should be viewed as a light reward-shaping layer rather than as a new RLHF training stack.

Computational overhead.

The additional burden is small. During autoregressive rollout, the model already returns the tokenwise conditional probabilities needed to form each completion probability π¯(k)=π¯​(y(k)∣x)\bar{\pi}^{(k)}=\bar{\pi}(y^{(k)}\mid x), so no extra model query is required; one only accumulates the emitted token probabilities along the sampled response. Once the proxy rewards are available, soft DRRO adds GG scalar exponentials, one normalization of the sampled rollout probabilities, and the corresponding reshaped rewards. Relative to sequence generation, reward-model scoring, and the usual minibatch policy-gradient updates, these operations are negligible. This is the operational reason why the DRRO modification fits naturally into mature GRPO codebases.

Choice of ambiguity geometry.

The choice of the ℓ1\ell_{1} ambiguity set is equally practical. The promptwise adversary has a dual-norm form for general ℓp\ell_{p} geometry, but ℓ1\ell_{1} is the case that turns this structure into a water-filling policy and a sampled RLHF bonus. In the algorithm, its key advantage is locality: the robust correction can be written in terms of the probability assigned to the threatening sampled response rather than the entire hidden simplex. The next proposition makes this statement precise by comparing ℓp\ell_{p} ambiguity geometries through the bonus factor attached to a vertex response.

Proposition 4.5 (Endpoint norms and coordinate-local sampled bonuses).

Fix n≥3n\geq 3. Suppose the promptwise ambiguity set is ‖Δ‖p≤δ\left\lVert\Delta\right\rVert_{p}\leq\delta and let p∗p^{\ast} be the dual exponent satisfying 1/p+1/p∗=11/p+1/p^{\ast}=1. Then

Ψp​(π,r^)\displaystyle\Psi_{p}(\pi;\hat{r}) :=max‖Δ‖p≤δ⁡Reg⁡(π,r^+Δ),\displaystyle:=\max_{\left\lVert\Delta\right\rVert_{p}\leq\delta}\Reg(\pi,\hat{r}+\Delta), (4.14)
Ψp​(π,r^)\displaystyle\Psi_{p}(\pi;\hat{r}) =maxi⁡{r^i−⟨π,r^⟩+δ​bp,i​(π)},\displaystyle=\max_{i}\left\{\hat{r}_{i}-\left\langle\pi,\hat{r}\right\rangle+\delta b_{p,i}(\pi)\right\},
bp,i​(π)\displaystyle b_{p,i}(\pi) ≔‖ei−π‖p∗.\displaystyle\coloneqq\left\lVert e_{i}-\pi\right\rVert_{p^{\ast}}.

The vertex bonus factor bp,i​(π)b_{p,i}(\pi) depends only on the sampled-coordinate probability πi\pi_{i} for all π∈Δn\pi\in\Delta_{n} if and only if p∈{1,∞}p\in\{1,\infty\}. In those endpoint cases,

b1,i​(π)=1−πi,b∞,i​(π)=2​(1−πi).b_{1,i}(\pi)=1-\pi_{i},\qquad b_{\infty,i}(\pi)=2(1-\pi_{i}).

Consequently, ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} ambiguity induces the same promptwise policy dependence as ℓ1\ell_{1} ambiguity after doubling the budget:

max‖Δ‖∞≤δ⁡Reg⁡(π,r^+Δ)=2​δ+maxi⁡{r^i−2​δ​πi}−⟨π,r^⟩.\max_{\left\lVert\Delta\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\delta}\Reg(\pi,\hat{r}+\Delta)=2\delta+\max_{i}\{\hat{r}_{i}-2\delta\pi_{i}\}-\left\langle\pi,\hat{r}\right\rangle.

The proposition has a useful interpretation. For any nonendpoint norm 1<p<∞1<p<\infty, a sampled response cannot be assigned a robust bonus from its own rollout probability alone: the bonus also depends on how the policy distributes probability across all other, mostly unobserved responses. The two endpoint geometries are exceptional. The case p=∞p=\infty is coordinate-local too, but it is essentially the same policy correction as ℓ1\ell_{1} after multiplying the budget by two, while its adversarial perturbation is dense rather than sparse. We therefore use ℓ1\ell_{1}: it gives the local sampled bonus needed for implementation, keeps the worst-case reward perturbation concentrated on the threatening response, and gives the budget the direct meaning of total promptwise reward misspecification mass. Once the response space is only partially observed through grouped rollouts, this sparse and local structure is exactly what makes the DRRO correction estimable.

5 Experiments

This section reports the empirical study of DRRO for RLHF. The experiments are designed to isolate the decision-theoretic question studied in the paper: when a policy is optimized against an imperfect proxy reward, does regret robustness preserve useful improvement better than value robustness and other mitigation strategies?

Setup.

All methods use the same VERL-based RLHF stack (Sheng et al., 2024) with Ray workers (Moritz et al., 2018) and vLLM rollout (Kwon et al., 2023). We use HuggingFaceH4/hh-rlhf (Bai et al., 2022) as prompts, Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2024a) as the policy, a fine-tuned OpenAssistant DeBERTa-v3-base reward model (He et al., 2021; OpenAssistant, 2023a) as the proxy reward, and the Tasksource DeBERTa-v3-large RLHF reward model (Sileo, 2023) as the held-out evaluator. Performance is reward improvement over the initial policy: for evaluator revalr_{\mathrm{eval}}, we report 𝔼⁡[reval​(x,Yπ)]−𝔼⁡[reval​(x,Yπ0)]\mathbb{E}[r_{\mathrm{eval}}(x,Y_{\pi})]-\mathbb{E}[r_{\mathrm{eval}}(x,Y_{\pi_{0}})] on held-out prompts. “Proxy” is the training reward model; “gold” is the separate held-out reward model. The gold evaluator is never used for policy updates. Appendix G gives fine-tuning, proxy-quality, implementation, and hyperparameter details.

The main benchmark sits at intermediate proxy quality: the fine-tuned proxy has 85.7% pairwise agreement with the held-out evaluator, between the raw-proxy stress test (73.6%) and large-proxy sanity check (95.2%) in Appendix G. All reported main curves average five seeds, with shaded regions showing one standard deviation across seeds. Rewards are reported as improvements relative to the step-0 initial policy; proxy and gold improvements are each re-centered by their own step-0 baseline. The horizontal axis is sequence-level KL from the frozen initial policy, estimated on sampled completions from the current policy; the exact estimator is given in Appendix G. This KL is logged only for diagnostics and plotting and is not an explicit penalty in the training loss.

Benchmark methods.

The comparison isolates value-versus-regret robustness while including common over-optimization mitigations. PPO is the standard clipped actor-critic baseline (Schulman et al., 2017); GRPO removes the critic and uses grouped within-prompt reward normalization (Shao et al., 2024). Ensemble-Mean and Ensemble-UWO follow reward-model ensemble mitigation (Coste et al., 2024; Eisenstein et al., 2024): the former averages reward models, while the latter subtracts ensemble disagreement. BSPO discourages movement into out-of-distribution responses (Dai et al., 2025), and InfoRM represents reward-proxy improvement through information-theoretic reward modeling (Miao et al., 2024). DRO-RLHF implements the standard value-robust benchmark (Ben-Tal et al., 2013; Wiesemann et al., 2014; Mohajerin Esfahani and Kuhn, 2018) with the same rollout and budget interface as DRRO. DRRO-RLHF is evaluated in a hard sampled-bonus variant, which gives the robust bonus to the sampled completion with largest r^(k)−δ~​π~(k)\widehat{r}^{(k)}-\widetilde{\delta}\,\widetilde{\pi}^{(k)}, and in the soft dynamic-budget variant from Section 4.

For the robust methods, DRO and DRRO receive the same budget information; only the robust benchmark changes. The default fixed scaled budget is δ~=2.5​G\widetilde{\delta}=2.5G, and the displayed soft-dynamic DRRO setting uses dynamic coefficient α=10\alpha=10 and soft-assignment temperature τ=2.0\tau=2.0. Dynamic-budget runs use (4.13).

Main comparison.

Figures 3 and 1 show the central pattern. The figure gives reward-versus-KL trajectories, and the table reports each method’s best held-out gold point with its proxy value, gold-proxy gap, and KL from the initial policy. PPO and GRPO make early progress, but proxy and gold separate as KL grows; DRRO attains the largest peak gold reward while maintaining a smaller gold-proxy gap than the strongest proxy-chasing baselines.

Numerically, soft dynamic DRRO reaches peak gold reward 1.431.43, above GRPO (1.271.27), PPO (1.201.20), and hard DRRO (1.171.17), at moderate KL 32.4732.47 and with the smallest strong-method gold-proxy gap (−1.10-1.10). GRPO, BSPO, and InfoRM can have larger proxy-at-peak values but larger negative gaps, so DRRO’s improvement is not proxy chasing. DRO has similar KL to DRRO (33.2633.26 versus 32.4732.47) but only 0.790.79 peak gold, illustrating value-robust over-pessimism. Thus Figure 3 should be read as a frontier plot, while Figure 4(a) isolates the value-robust baseline.

DRO and ablations.

Figure 4(a) isolates the value-versus-regret benchmark. DRO and DRRO use the same rollout stack and budget information, but DRO pessimizes absolute value while DRRO pessimizes regret. This empirical gap anticipates the theoretical comparison in Section 6: value robustness can be too conservative because it protects a policy in isolation, whereas regret robustness protects the comparison that actually drives the decision. Figure 4(b) shows that both DRRO design choices matter: soft assignment avoids committing to one noisy completion, while dynamic budgeting grows ambiguity with KL drift. The four DRRO variants in Figure 4(b) use hyperparameters selected by the grid search described in Appendix G; the hard-max ablation algorithm is detailed in Section G.1.

6 Comparing DRO and DRRO

The experiments make the value-versus-regret distinction visible before the theory names it. DRO protects absolute value and can therefore become conservative even when the proxy still contains useful comparative information. DRRO protects regret, so its pessimism is relative to the policies that compete under the same plausible reward perturbation. This section formalizes that difference through two lenses: rank preservation and local coverage.

6.1 Rank-Preserving Proxy Rewards

Pairwise reward-model training is fundamentally ordinal. Bradley–Terry-style objectives and modern RLHF reward-model pipelines learn scores by assigning larger values to preferred responses than to rejected ones (Bradley and Terry, 1952; Christiano et al., 2017; Stiennon et al., 2020; Ouyang et al., 2022). This is why held-out pairwise accuracy and ranking correlation remain standard diagnostics (Lambert et al., 2025), even though accuracy alone does not determine downstream RLHF performance (Chen et al., 2024). A natural test is therefore whether the robust objective can exploit a proxy ranking that is correct but not perfectly calibrated.

For the fixed-prompt ℓ1\ell_{1} specialization used by the water-filling rule and the algorithm, promptwise DRO solves

maxπ∈Δn⁡⟨π,r^⟩−δ​‖π‖∞.\max_{\pi\in\Delta_{n}}\ \left\langle\pi,\hat{r}\right\rangle-\delta\left\lVert\pi\right\rVert_{\infty}.

The penalty is blind to which responses the proxy ranks highest. DRRO keeps that ordering inside the regret term. The next theorem shows that, under rank preservation, this difference translates into higher true value.

Theorem 6.1 (DRRO dominates DRO under rank-preserving truth).

Assume the proxy reward is strictly ordered,

r^1>r^2>⋯>r^n,\hat{r}_{1}>\hat{r}_{2}>\cdots>\hat{r}_{n},

and that the true reward is a rank-preserving transform of the proxy reward,

ti=ϕ(r^i),i=1,…,n,t_{i}=\phi(\hat{r}_{i}),\qquad i=1,\ldots,n,

for some increasing function ϕ\phi. Let

πDRO​(δ)∈arg​maxπ∈Δn⁡{⟨π,r^⟩−δ​‖π‖∞},\pi^{\mathrm{DRO}}(\delta)\in\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\pi\in\Delta_{n}}\left\{\left\langle\pi,\hat{r}\right\rangle-\delta\left\lVert\pi\right\rVert_{\infty}\right\},

and

πDRRO​(δ)∈arg​maxπ∈Δn⁡{⟨π,r^⟩−maxi⁡(r^i−δ​πi)}.\pi^{\mathrm{DRRO}}(\delta)\in\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\pi\in\Delta_{n}}\left\{\left\langle\pi,\hat{r}\right\rangle-\max_{i}(\hat{r}_{i}-\delta\pi_{i})\right\}.

Then

∑i=1nπiDRRO​(δ)​ti≥∑i=1nπiDRO​(δ)​ti.\sum_{i=1}^{n}\pi_{i}^{\mathrm{DRRO}}(\delta)\,t_{i}\geq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\pi_{i}^{\mathrm{DRO}}(\delta)\,t_{i}.

If ϕ\phi is strictly increasing and the two optimizers differ, then the displayed inequality is strict.

The proof in Appendix H shows that the DRRO optimizer majorizes the DRO optimizer. DRO equalizes exposure because it protects worst-case value; DRRO reallocates mass only when doing so reduces regret against plausible competitors. When the proxy ranking is correct, DRRO therefore preserves more mass on the best-ranked responses.

6.2 Coverage as an Alternative View

The rank-preserving theorem isolates a promptwise mechanism. A complementary view asks what the robust guarantees pay for after prompts and reward uncertainty are aggregated. Because Figure 3 shows that all methods can deteriorate after drifting too far from the initial policy, we compare DRO and DRRO inside a local policy class.

Let d⁡(π,π0)\mathrm{d}(\pi,\pi_{0}) be a policy-drift statistic, with the expected KL divergence to the initial policy as the canonical RLHF example, and define the local policy class

Πρ:={π∈Π:d⁡(π,π0)≤ρ}.\Pi_{\rho}:=\{\pi\in\Pi:\mathrm{d}(\pi,\pi_{0})\leq\rho\}.

This captures the trust-region viewpoint without adding a KL penalty to the objective. For each prompt xx, let zπ​(x)z_{\pi}(x) be a linear policy representation: in the finite-response case, zπ(x)=π(⋅∣x)z_{\pi}(x)=\pi(\cdot\mid x); in sequential settings, it can be an occupancy measure. Then

Jr​(π)=𝔼x∼𝒟​[⟨zπ​(x),r⁡(x)⟩].J_{r}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\big[\left\langle z_{\pi}(x),r(x)\right\rangle\big].

Let μx\mu_{x} be a full-support coverage distribution, such as the behavior distribution induced by reward-model training data. Following the concentrability logic common in offline RL (Munos and Szepesvári, 2008; Zhan et al., 2022), and keeping the geometry aligned with the promptwise ℓ1\ell_{1} model, define

‖e‖1,μx:=∑y∈𝒴μx​(y)​|e⁡(y)|,‖v‖∞,μx−1:=maxy∈𝒴⁡|v⁡(y)|μx​(y),\left\lVert e\right\rVert_{1,\mu_{x}}:=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\mu_{x}(y)|e(y)|,\qquad\left\lVert v\right\rVert_{\infty,\mu_{x}^{-1}}:=\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\frac{|v(y)|}{\mu_{x}(y)},

where μx​(y)>0\mu_{x}(y)>0 for every response yy. Assume the mean weighted ℓ1\ell_{1} confidence set

𝒰ε(1):={r:𝔼x∼𝒟​[‖r⁡(x)−r^​(x)‖1,μx]≤ε}.\mathcal{U}^{(1)}_{\varepsilon}:=\left\{r:\ \mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\big[\left\lVert r(x)-\hat{r}(x)\right\rVert_{1,\mu_{x}}\big]\leq\varepsilon\right\}.

This integrated condition is implied by the pointwise promptwise ℓ1\ell_{1} ambiguity condition in the algorithmic specialization, since μx\mu_{x} is a probability distribution.

Define

πρDRO\displaystyle\pi_{\rho}^{\mathrm{DRO}} ∈arg​maxπ∈Πρ⁡minr∈𝒰ε(1)⁡Jr​(π),\displaystyle\in\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\pi\in\Pi_{\rho}}\ \min_{r\in\mathcal{U}^{(1)}_{\varepsilon}}J_{r}(\pi),
πρDRRO\displaystyle\pi_{\rho}^{\mathrm{DRRO}} ∈arg​minπ∈Πρ⁡maxr∈𝒰ε(1)⁡[maxβ∈Πρ⁡Jr​(β)−Jr​(π)].\displaystyle\in\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{\pi\in\Pi_{\rho}}\ \max_{r\in\mathcal{U}^{(1)}_{\varepsilon}}\Big[\max_{\beta\in\Pi_{\rho}}J_{r}(\beta)-J_{r}(\pi)\Big].

Let πρ⋆∈arg​maxπ∈Πρ⁡Jr⋆​(π)\pi_{\rho}^{\star}\in\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\pi\in\Pi_{\rho}}J_{r^{\star}}(\pi) denote the best local policy under the true reward.

For DRO, the relevant quantity is absolute exposure.

Definition 6.2 (Absolute integrated concentrability).

For a policy π∈Πρ\pi\in\Pi_{\rho}, define

C∞​(π,μ,𝒟):=ess​supx∼𝒟⁡‖zπ​(x)‖∞,μx−1.C_{\infty}(\pi;\mu,\mathcal{D}):=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\left\lVert z_{\pi}(x)\right\rVert_{\infty,\mu_{x}^{-1}}.

This is the product-space weighted ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} dual of the mean ℓ1\ell_{1} reward-error set. It yields the following absolute-value certificate.

Proposition 6.3 (DRO certificate).

For every π∈Πρ\pi\in\Pi_{\rho},

minr∈𝒰ε(1)⁡Jr​(π)=Jr^​(π)−ε​C∞​(π,μ,𝒟).\min_{r\in\mathcal{U}^{(1)}_{\varepsilon}}J_{r}(\pi)=J_{\hat{r}}(\pi)-\varepsilon C_{\infty}(\pi;\mu,\mathcal{D}). (6.1)

The same certificate yields a local regret guarantee.

Proposition 6.4 (DRO regret bound).

Suppose r⋆∈𝒰ε(1)r^{\star}\in\mathcal{U}^{(1)}_{\varepsilon}. Then

Jr⋆​(πρ⋆)−Jr⋆​(πρDRO)≤2​ε​C∞​(πρ⋆,μ,𝒟).J_{r^{\star}}(\pi_{\rho}^{\star})-J_{r^{\star}}(\pi_{\rho}^{\mathrm{DRO}})\leq 2\varepsilon C_{\infty}(\pi_{\rho}^{\star};\mu,\mathcal{D}). (6.2)

For DRRO, uncertainty enters through policy differences.

Definition 6.5 (Relative integrated concentrability).

For policies π,β∈Πρ\pi,\beta\in\Pi_{\rho}, define

C∞,rel​(β,π,μ,𝒟):=ess​supx∼𝒟⁡‖zβ​(x)−zπ​(x)‖∞,μx−1.C_{\infty,\mathrm{rel}}(\beta,\pi;\mu,\mathcal{D}):=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\left\lVert z_{\beta}(x)-z_{\pi}(x)\right\rVert_{\infty,\mu_{x}^{-1}}.

This relative coefficient is the object that appears in regret.

Proposition 6.6 (DRRO certificate).

For every π∈Πρ\pi\in\Pi_{\rho},

maxr∈𝒰ε(1)⁡[maxβ∈Πρ⁡Jr​(β)−Jr​(π)]\displaystyle\max_{r\in\mathcal{U}^{(1)}_{\varepsilon}}\Big[\max_{\beta\in\Pi_{\rho}}J_{r}(\beta)-J_{r}(\pi)\Big] (6.3)
=maxβ∈Πρ⁡{Jr^​(β)−Jr^​(π)+ε​C∞,rel​(β,π,μ,𝒟)}.\displaystyle=\max_{\beta\in\Pi_{\rho}}\left\{J_{\hat{r}}(\beta)-J_{\hat{r}}(\pi)+\varepsilon C_{\infty,\mathrm{rel}}(\beta,\pi;\mu,\mathcal{D})\right\}.

The guarantee depends only on comparators that can be optimal for some reward in the confidence set. Define

Πρ⋆​(𝒰ε(1)):=⋃r∈𝒰ε(1)arg​maxπ∈Πρ⁡Jr​(π),\Pi_{\rho}^{\star}(\mathcal{U}^{(1)}_{\varepsilon}):=\bigcup_{r\in\mathcal{U}^{(1)}_{\varepsilon}}\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\pi\in\Pi_{\rho}}J_{r}(\pi),

and the localized relative-concentrability radius at a candidate policy π\pi

𝒞∞,rel​(𝒰ε(1),π,μ,𝒟):=maxβ∈Πρ⋆​(𝒰ε(1))⁡C∞,rel​(β,π,μ,𝒟).\mathcal{C}_{\infty,\mathrm{rel}}(\mathcal{U}^{(1)}_{\varepsilon},\pi;\mu,\mathcal{D}):=\max_{\beta\in\Pi_{\rho}^{\star}(\mathcal{U}^{(1)}_{\varepsilon})}C_{\infty,\mathrm{rel}}(\beta,\pi;\mu,\mathcal{D}).
Proposition 6.7 (DRRO regret bound with localized relative concentrability).

Suppose r⋆∈𝒰ε(1)r^{\star}\in\mathcal{U}^{(1)}_{\varepsilon}. Then

Jr⋆​(πρ⋆)−Jr⋆​(πρDRRO)≤2​ε​𝒞∞,rel​(𝒰ε(1),πρ⋆,μ,𝒟).J_{r^{\star}}(\pi_{\rho}^{\star})-J_{r^{\star}}(\pi_{\rho}^{\mathrm{DRRO}})\leq 2\varepsilon\mathcal{C}_{\infty,\mathrm{rel}}(\mathcal{U}^{(1)}_{\varepsilon},\pi_{\rho}^{\star};\mu,\mathcal{D}).
Remark 6.8 (Comparison between DRO and DRRO regret bounds).

DRO pays for absolute concentrability, while DRRO pays for relative concentrability between the chosen policy and plausible local comparators. For a fixed prompt, the relative term is

maxy∈𝒴⁡|zβ​(x,y)−zπ​(x,y)|μx​(y),\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\frac{|z_{\beta}(x,y)-z_{\pi}(x,y)|}{\mu_{x}(y)},

which can cancel common exposure shared by nearby policies. The reverse triangle inequality and the triangle inequality give

C∞​(π,μ,𝒟)−C∞​(β,μ,𝒟)≤C∞,rel​(β,π,μ,𝒟)≤C∞​(π,μ,𝒟)+C∞​(β,μ,𝒟).C_{\infty}(\pi;\mu,\mathcal{D})-C_{\infty}(\beta;\mu,\mathcal{D})\leq C_{\infty,\mathrm{rel}}(\beta,\pi;\mu,\mathcal{D})\leq C_{\infty}(\pi;\mu,\mathcal{D})+C_{\infty}(\beta;\mu,\mathcal{D}).

Writing ℬε≔Πρ⋆​(𝒰ε(1))\mathcal{B}_{\varepsilon}\coloneqq\Pi_{\rho}^{\star}(\mathcal{U}^{(1)}_{\varepsilon}), C⁡(γ)≔C∞​(γ,μ,𝒟)C(\gamma)\coloneqq C_{\infty}(\gamma;\mu,\mathcal{D}), and ℭ⁡(π)≔𝒞∞,rel​(𝒰ε(1),π,μ,𝒟)\mathfrak{C}(\pi)\coloneqq\mathcal{C}_{\infty,\mathrm{rel}}(\mathcal{U}^{(1)}_{\varepsilon},\pi;\mu,\mathcal{D}), maximizing over β∈ℬε\beta\in\mathcal{B}_{\varepsilon} gives

C⁡(π)−minβ∈ℬε⁡C⁡(β)≤ℭ⁡(π)≤C⁡(π)+maxβ∈ℬε⁡C⁡(β).C(\pi)-\min_{\beta\in\mathcal{B}_{\varepsilon}}C(\beta)\leq\mathfrak{C}(\pi)\leq C(\pi)+\max_{\beta\in\mathcal{B}_{\varepsilon}}C(\beta).

For a fixed confidence set, the comparator-side extrema are constants. Thus DRO behaves like optimizing with an absolute policy-exposure penalty, while DRRO uses the largest relative exposure to plausible comparators. The absolute-exposure view is a triangle-inequality envelope of the relative one, explaining why DRO regret guarantees can be looser.

7 Conclusion

RLHF is optimization under a misspecified reward: the policy is trained against a learned proxy, but deployment quality is judged by latent human preferences. The key modeling choice is therefore where to place pessimism. We argue that regret is the right target. Worst-case value protects a policy in isolation; worst-case regret compares it with the hindsight-best policy under the same plausible reward, matching the loss induced by objective misspecification more directly.

Under norm-induced Wasserstein ambiguity, the promptwise RLHF problem admits a dual-norm closed-form adversary. In the ℓ1\ell_{1} specialization, this structure further yields a water-filling optimal policy and a coordinate-local bonus that can be translated into a GRPO-compatible reward-shaping algorithm with light computational overhead. Empirically, the resulting DRRO correction mitigates over-optimization more effectively than the tested baselines, while standard value-robust DRO is systematically over-pessimistic.

8 Code and Data Disclosure

An anonymized implementation is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/status/DRRO_anonymous-1E42. It contains the DRRO-GRPO training code, requirements, launch scripts, and reproduction instructions.

The experiments use open-source assets: prompts from Hugging Face H4 HH-RLHF, derived from Anthropic HH-RLHF (Bai et al., 2022); Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct as the initial policy (Qwen Team, 2024a; Qwen Team, 2024b); OpenAssistant DeBERTa-v3 reward models as proxies (He et al., 2021; OpenAssistant, 2023a; OpenAssistant, 2023b); and the Tasksource DeBERTa-v3-large RLHF reward model as the held-out evaluator (Sileo, 2023). We do not redistribute modified datasets or model checkpoints; URLs and implementation details are provided in the repository and Appendix G.

Appendix B Literature Review

RLHF and objective misspecification.

RLHF emerged from the preference-learning framework of Christiano et al. [2017], who used human comparisons to train reward functions for reinforcement learning agents. Ziegler et al. [2019] and Stiennon et al. [2020] adapted that logic to language modeling and summarization, while Ouyang et al. [2022] turned it into the now-standard LLM pipeline of supervised fine-tuning, reward modeling, and reference-anchored policy optimization, often implemented with KL control. Direct preference methods such as DPO [Rafailov et al., 2023] eliminate the explicit reward-model optimization stage, but they do not eliminate the underlying problem of learning from a finite proxy for human preference. Among recent surveys, Kaufmann et al. [2025] provide a broad map of RLHF across domains, Chaudhari et al. [2024] focus on reward-model misspecification in LLM alignment, and Liu et al. [2026] emphasize preference learning, uncertainty quantification, and statistical inference.

Over-optimization and mitigation strategies.

The empirical evidence is now fairly systematic. Gao et al. [2023] document the canonical proxy-versus-gold divergence in RLHF; Rafailov et al. [2024] show that the same phenomenon persists in direct alignment algorithms; and Hosking et al. [2024] argue that human-feedback scores themselves can be misaligned with true quality because they over-reward stylistic features such as assertiveness. On the mitigation side, one family of papers tries to improve the reward model itself. Coste et al. [2024] and Eisenstein et al. [2024] study reward-model ensembles as a hedge against reward hacking; Miao et al. [2024] use an information-theoretic reward-model objective; Yang et al. [2024] regularize hidden states to improve generalization; Liu et al. [2025] target artifact robustness; and Bukharin et al. [2025] generate adversarial hard examples for reward-model training. A related line updates the reward model as the policy moves, including the iterative preference-learning method of Xiong et al. [2024], the active preference-optimization framework of Das et al. [2024], and the off-policy correction of Ackermann et al. [2025].

A second family leaves the reward model largely intact but modifies the policy objective. Zhai et al. [2024] penalize reward uncertainty estimated from LoRA ensembles, Xu et al. [2025] learn a pessimistic reward model, and Yan et al. [2024] optimize a reward-robust policy objective. A third family regularizes the policy toward regions where the reward model is thought to be reliable. Moskovitz et al. [2024] impose explicit constraints in RLHF, Dai et al. [2025] regularize toward behavior-supported regions, Rita et al. [2024] use demonstration-guided reinforcement learning, and Liu et al. [2024] show that SFT loss can play the role of an adversarial regularizer. These methods are important points of comparison for us because they reveal the central tension: protecting against reward misspecification is valuable, but methods built around pessimistic value or hard feasible-region restrictions can also suppress useful policy improvement. Xu et al. [2025] make this concern explicit by arguing that KL-based regularization can exclude high-performing policies with large KL divergence, and Li et al. [2025] show that divergence-based bonuses can reinforce conservative behavior rather than encourage exploration of uncertain but promising regions.

DRO and DRRO in operations research.

Standard DRO protects decisions against ambiguity in probabilities, distributions, and objective coefficients. Ben-Tal et al. [2013] study robust solutions under uncertain probabilities, Wiesemann et al. [2014] provide a general convex-optimization framework, Mohajerin Esfahani and Kuhn [2018] develop data-driven Wasserstein DRO, Blanchet and Murthy [2019] quantify distributional model risk, and Rahimian and Mehrotra [2019] survey the area. The concern that worst-case value may be overly conservative leads naturally to regret-based robustness. Averbakh [2004] and Averbakh and Lebedev [2005] develop classical minmax-regret models and complexity results; Chen and Xie [2021] study regret in the newsvendor problem; and Agarwal and Zhang [2022], Cho and Yang [2024], Bitar [2024], and Fiechtner and Blanchet [2025] develop distributionally robust regret formulations in modern statistical and learning settings. Our paper imports that line of work into RLHF and shows that the regret benchmark becomes especially natural once reward uncertainty, rather than transition uncertainty, is the main source of misspecification.

Appendix C Discussion on KL Penalty Term

The KL term should nevertheless be interpreted carefully, because it remains a common reference point in RLHF. For a suitable multiplier η\eta, the penalized formulation is the Lagrangian form of the trust-region problem

maxπ∈ΠJr^(π)subject to𝔼x∼𝒟[KL(π(⋅∣x)∥π0(⋅∣x))]≤ε.\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\ J_{\hat{r}}(\pi)\qquad\text{subject to}\qquad\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\!\left[\mathrm{KL}\!\big(\pi(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{0}(\cdot\mid x)\big)\right]\leq\varepsilon.

Thus KL control is one way to mitigate over-optimization by shrinking the feasible policy set around the reference model. That safeguard can be useful, but it is not intrinsic to RLHF and it is no longer the only practical recipe. Recent large-scale LLM-RL implementations already train successfully without an explicit KL penalty: Hu et al. [2025] show that vanilla PPO with rule-based rewards can scale reasoning performance without any KL regularization, while Yu et al. [2025] explicitly remove the KL term from GRPO-style long-chain-of-thought training and argue that large divergence from the initial model need not be suppressed when it supports better reasoning.

More importantly, KL control is not exactly to the point for the misspecification problem studied here. If the raw proxy reward is imperfect, then maximizing that same proxy over a smaller KL ball is still a constrained optimization against a misspecified objective. In that sense, KL regularization is a last-resort hedge: it limits how much damage the proxy can do by limiting how far the policy may move, but it does not repair the proxy itself. Our viewpoint is that a more direct mitigation is to improve the reward signal being optimized. Once a robust correction is added to the proxy reward, optimizing the corrected surrogate over a given feasible region is more natural than preserving the uncorrected proxy and relying on the feasible-region restriction alone.

Appendix D Mean-Reward Reduction and Promptwise Ambiguity

Proof of Proposition 2.1.

By Fubini’s theorem,

JP​(π)\displaystyle J_{P}(\pi) =𝔼R∼P𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼π(⋅∣x)[R(x,y)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{R\sim P}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\ y\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x)}[R(x,y)]
=𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼π(⋅∣x)𝔼R∼P[R(x,y)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\ y\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x)}\mathbb{E}_{R\sim P}[R(x,y)]
=𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼π(⋅∣x)[r¯P(x,y)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\ y\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x)}[\bar{r}_{P}(x,y)]
=Jr¯P​(π).\displaystyle=J_{\bar{r}_{P}}(\pi).

Thus the ex-ante DRRO objective sees a distribution over reward functions only through its mean reward. ∎
